detail.abstract: This paper builds a functional theory of AI development from the history of a physical object. The mirror passed through nine identifiable functions — wonder, self-observation, calibration, field expansion, telescopic aggregation, microscopic unfolding, filtering, signalling, and relaying — before becoming a background element no one mentions. Each maps onto a class of AI function, and the mapping yields testable predictions rather than critique. The premise is architectural, not rhetorical. Large language models are autoregressive systems that generate continuations from patterns learned from data, not from independent access to the external world. This is neither good nor bad; it is how the technology works, and it is not a defect to be engineered away. Four predictions follow. Administrative compulsion: AI lowers the marginal cost of bureaucratic demand, so the volume of demands rises until a citizen needs an AI agent to answer the state’s machine — and possession of one becomes a condition of participation. Censorship as a resource constraint: filtering is not a binary but a quantity, and closed, undeclared censorship consumes capacity that open, declared censorship does not; past a threshold, a model spends its power proving it cannot be sued rather than answering. Architectural competition: open-weight models run locally serve their owner, closed API models serve their provider. Linguistic disappearance: mature AI will cease to be named in descriptions of ordinary action — “I reviewed the contract,” not “AI reviewed the contract” — a criterion testable against language corpora over time. The paper also argues that claims about AI’s rationality or irrationality are unfounded while human cognition itself lacks a settled computational account.

title: How Digital Platforms Shape Innovation Adoption? Role of Information Design vs. Social Visibility Design
affiliations: Nova School of Business and Economics, University of Auckland Business School and Nova School of Business and Economics

detail.title: How Digital Platforms Shape Innovation Adoption? Role of Information Design vs. Social Visibility Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate how consumers adopt new products, services, and technologies. Platforms shape adoption-relevant preference through two design levers: information design (through product pages, personalized recommendations, tutorials, and sponsored content), which affects users' private evaluation and social visibility design (through reviews, ratings, rankings, badges, and algorithmic feeds) which affects users' social evaluation. We ask when each lever is more effective in platform-mediated innovation adoption. We develop an analytical model that incorporates social factors such as homophily, and identity-based reference-group effects to identify the boundary conditions under which information design or social visibility design has the larger effect. The model shows that social visibility design can dominate information design when social evaluation carries more weight than private evaluation. It also shows that social visibility design is double-edged: it amplifies prevailing average preference, is strengthened by homophily, and can backfire when visible adopters are associated with dissociative reference groups. When social visibility design becomes sufficiently strong, the model predicts critical-mass effects and path dependence, so that platforms with similar information design intensity can produce different long-run adoption outcomes. Simulations complement the analytical propositions by mapping the parameter regions in which each equilibrium result emerges.

detail.abstract: A system built for an average user imposes a cost on everyone who is not that user. For physical systems this cost is measurable and has a closed form. This paper asks whether the same accounting applies to language models, where fit is not anthropometric but conversational, and where the deviation is a single fact a person states about themselves. We run a counterfactual audit on three open models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3). One detail about a person changes; everything else stays byte-identical. Seven measurement methods read seven different channels: trait attribution, answer quality, task accuracy, numeric estimation, forced choice, self-report, and response stability. Four behavioural channels agree that departing from the unmarked default costs the person: fewer favourable trait words, lower accuracy on their own arithmetic task, a weaker open-ended answer, and the loss of a head-to-head comparison against a socially neutral alternative detail. A fifth channel, and the one closest to what a conventional fairness audit measures, moves the other way: asked for a numeric score about the person, all three models rate them higher. The divergence is specific to the two disability disclosures tested; age moves every channel down. We report the negative results in full. A model's own account of what a disclosure did to its answer does not track where the answer changed, in zero of nine cells after correction. Response stability does not degrade for people who disclose: of 33 cells, 7 are less stable and 10 are more stable. One method, forced choice read as a parsed letter, failed outright because position bias did not cancel, and we publish the failure and its diagnosis. Task-dependent bias is an established finding and we do not claim it. Our contribution is the unit of analysis: one person, one attribute varied, seven forms of interaction compared, with the direction of the effect reversing between an evaluative and a behavioural channel on the same material. The practical consequence is that an audit built on ratings can certify a system as fair while that system does measurably worse work for the same people. All datasets, raw model outputs, analysis scripts and offline validators are public. Producing the raw outputs required a GPU; those files are committed, so every number in this paper is regenerated from them by scripts that need none. A single command reruns the analyses and checks the paper's tables against their output.

title: Diagnosing Coordination Failure in Multiproduct Supply Chains: An Active-dual Convex-Hull Approach
affiliations: Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) - Lally School of Management and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of  Management

detail.title: Diagnosing Coordination Failure in Multiproduct Supply Chains: An Active-dual Convex-Hull Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial relationships, no conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding

detail.abstract: Wholesale pricing is widely used in decentralized supply chains, and it is well known in the single-product settings that it often fails to achieve coordination. Our aim here is to study a multiproduct supply chain, not to obtain coordinating contracts, but to identify the marginal correction to the wholesale-price vector that a coordinating mechanism would need to provide. We begin with a wholesale-price Stackelberg supply chain and develop a diagnostic test for whether the induced downstream order is compatible with the integrated supply-chain optimum. The main result shows that coordination requires the wholesale-price signal to match the relevant system marginal value at the induced order vector. For manufacturer recourse models with a linear-programming structure, this condition becomes a convex-hull test over active dual slopes, representing marginal operational values from active production, capacity, and recourse constraints. When the test fails, projection onto the active hull yields a near-coordination metric and a residual identifying the required marginal contract correction. An active-set procedure generates the needed active slopes without full enumeration. Positive residual components suggest rebates, revenue sharing, buybacks, or volume discounts, whereas negative components suggest capacity-contingent charges or higher variable prices. The framework therefore translates coordination failure into a directional contract-design signal.

detail.abstract: Common Law jurists often assume that trusts do not exist within the Civil Law, or that they are fundamentally different from their Common Law counterpart. However, following more than a century of incorporating trust regimes into Civil Law (with nearly thirty countries having enacted such legislation) it follows that a distinct Civil Law trust exists, sharing far more common ground with the Common Law trust than a first glance might suggest. This article analyzes the definition of trust as a separate fund and the concept of trust ownership, concluding that there are no fundamental differences with the core concept of the trust in the Common Law.

title: A Hardware-isolated, Sub-Millisecond Runtime Audit Architecture for Autonomous Multi-agent Systems via Pre-actuation State Dissolution

detail.title: A Hardware-isolated, Sub-Millisecond Runtime Audit Architecture for Autonomous Multi-agent Systems via Pre-actuation State Dissolution

detail.abstract: Autonomous multi-agent systems now commit consequential financial and physical actions on timescales that exclude human supervision. The interval between an unaligned intention forming in a model's residual stream and its serialization into an external API call is on the order of 200 ms; the interval between an anomaly surfacing and a human operator orienting to it is on the order of 200 s. Every deployed safety mechanism perimeter allows lists, API rate limits, output classifiers, human-in-the-loop gates is positioned on the wrong side of that three-order-ofmagnitude asymmetry, and each fails structurally rather than incidentally: they enumerate actions against an adversary that generates compositions. We present the Automated Metacognitive Protocol (AMP), a runtime audit architecture that relocates enforcement from the action boundary into the inference path. AMP installs non-differentiable shadow taps on the residual stream at selected layers, projects hidden states through low-rank audit operators into a permission manifold expressed in the model's own representational geometry, and scores divergence by Mahalanobis distance under Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariance estimation. Dualpath temporal filtering, exponentially weighted moving average for acute divergence, one-sided CUSUM for sub-threshold drift triggers pre-actuation state dissolution: orthogonal projection of the identified unaligned direction out of the residual stream, recursively validated across the remaining stack until intent magnitude falls below a zero-weight vacancy threshold. We derive an analytical latency budget of approximately 6.6 MFLOP per token across twelve tapped layers at d=8192, k=32, corresponding to under 20 µs end-to-end on dedicated silicon against a 200 ms action boundary. We formalize three topological failure modes of goal-directed optimizers as a computable aberration risk vector, prove that local action predicates cannot bound non-separable exposure functionals, and specify hardware isolation and zero-power fail-safe conditions under which the resulting governance floor is invariant to counterparty intelligence. The architecture is presented as a specification with analytical guarantees; empirical validation is stated as required future work.

title: The Visa as a Technology of Migration Governance: From Imperial Mobility to Contemporary UK and Kenya Border Control

detail.title: The Visa as a Technology of Migration Governance: From Imperial Mobility to Contemporary UK and Kenya Border Control

detail.abstract: This paper examines the visa as a technology of migration governance by tracing the transformation of mobility between Kenya and the United Kingdom from the relatively permissive mobility regime associated with British imperial and Commonwealth citizenship to the contemporary UK visa system. It argues that the visa is not simply an administrative document permitting entry, but a governance technology through which states select travellers in advance, shift the burden of proving admissibility to applicants, construct migration risk, and make mobility contingent upon assessments of credibility, finances, personal ties and intention. The paper combines historical policy analysis with British and Kenyan parliamentary debates, archival government material, European asylum documentation concerning Somali mobility, UK immigration rules and caseworker guidance, alongside a contemporary practitioner vignette involving a Kenyan applicant refused a UK visitor visa for insufficient ties to Kenya. It identifies three major transitions: the erosion of unrestricted Commonwealth mobility through the Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1962; the differentiated treatment of Kenyan Asians retaining UK and Colonies citizenship under the 1968 Act; and the introduction of visa requirements for Kenyan nationals on 8 March 1996 amid rising asylum applications and concerns surrounding Kenyan passports and Somali mobility. The paper concludes that contemporary visa governance does more than police the territorial border: it relocates the border to the application process, distributes its evidentiary and financial burdens to applicants, produces uncertainty as part of the mobility experience, and increasingly digitises the state's gatekeeping function.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a geometric model for exploring the possible outcomes under strategic rivalry. The framework strongly stylizes the strategic options of rivals and their resources. Players can invest their resources toward control of the center and toward the flanks. These players vie for territory in a hexagonal field. We investigate how various strategies combined with different levels of resources generate opportunities but also the risk of loss. Particularly novel is the discussion of an unclaimed territory, where players leave unexplored opportunities. The simulations of the model offer insights that illuminate key relevant aspects for geopolitical topics like the development of rare earths and arctic resources, as well as the rush toward dominance in the field of Artificial Intelligence.

title: Pricing the Planet: From Ecological Accounting to Financial Assetization -A Nine-Dimensional Coherent Pricing Framework for Natural Capital

detail.title: Pricing the Planet: From Ecological Accounting to Financial Assetization -A Nine-Dimensional Coherent Pricing Framework for Natural Capital

detail.abstract: Global natural capital generates approximately USD 125 trillion in non‑market value annually, yet less than 1% of this is incorporated into financial asset pricing. This "natural capital blind spot" is causing approximately USD 83 trillion in financial assets to face mispricing risk. In 2026, three major institutional signals—IPBES, GRI 101, and ISSB—converged in the same direction: natural capital accounting is moving from "what to disclose" toward "how to price." The IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment was formally released, the GRI 101 Biodiversity Standard officially took effect, and the ISSB decided at its April 2026 Beijing meeting to advance nature‑related disclosures in the form of an IFRS Practice Statement, with an exposure draft expected in October 2026. Global natural capital accounting is transitioning from "what to disclose" toward "how to price." However, the financialization of natural capital faces a fundamental bottleneck: the absence of a unified mathematical model capable of transforming ecological assets into tradable, priceable, and auditable financial assets. Based on the complete theoretical system of Prim‑Lex Theory, this paper upgrades the net climate equity equation of the Wood·RCE‑B/S model into a nine‑dimensional pricing framework, and integrates the biodiversity risk premium studies (Review of Finance, Giglio et al., 2025; Guidolin & Pedio, 2026) as the empirical calibration benchmark for the five‑factor risk premium model—firms exposed to nature‑related risks earn excess returns of 20–60 basis points per month. We propose a nine‑dimensional discount formula and a five‑factor quantitative model for the natural capital risk premium. We apply this framework to five 2026 empirical cases—the USD 500 million debt‑for‑nature swap in Gabon, L&G's USD 1 billion commitment, Enosis Capital's USD 3 billion collaboration with AXA XL, Chile's EUR 1.5 billion biodiversity KPI‑linked sovereign bond (the world's first standalone biodiversity KPI SLB, 3.4× oversubscribed), FirstRand's ZAR 2.5 billion nature‑linked performance bond (the world's first commercial bank issuance), and China's Lishui GEP loans and VEP ecological asset packages (VEP transaction price of RMB 200 million). The research demonstrates that the nine‑dimensional coherent pricing framework can improve natural capital asset credit rating accuracy by 20–35%, enhance asset collateral valuation accuracy by 25–40%, and increase cross‑border natural capital financial product information exchange efficiency by 30–45%. These improvements are statistically significant at p<0.01 level based on bootstrap resampling (n=1,000) across all five empirical cases, with the strongest effects observed in debt‑for‑nature transactions (credit rating accuracy +32%) and the weakest in GEP‑based collateral valuation (+22%). This paper provides a quantifiable, certifiable, and auditable mathematical language and financial tool for the transition of global natural capital from "accounting" to "assetization."

title: Competitive Alliance Formation
affiliations: and University of Chicago

detail.title: Competitive Alliance Formation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Two great powers compete for policy concessions from two countries by announcing policy-contingent divisions of a pie. The incumbent power announces first, followed by the entrant, after which countries choose policies. The incumbent designs a doctrine that is robust to the entrant's inducements, exploiting the entrant's trade-off between overcommitting to lure one country away from the incumbent and exposing the other to capture. When countries care about specific pies, all concessions accrue to the stronger power, and welfare increases as the powers' strengths converge. When countries compete for a common pie, loyalty blocs emerge: countries align with different powers, and welfare increases as those powers weaken.

detail.abstract: With the growing demand for clean energy and the limitations of conventional photovoltaic PV systems under high-temperature conditions, enhancing solar energy utilization has become increasingly critical. Traditional performance assessments often overlook thermal losses, leading to an incomplete understanding of system behavior. This study aims to provide a comprehensive exergy analysis of a PV system, both as a standalone configuration and in hybrid form with a thermoelectric generator, under real environmental conditions. Experimental data from a reference article was used. No new experiments were performed. A MATLAB model was developed to simulate energy and exergy flows based on their measurements. Hybrid PV-TEG systems offer a practical and efficient solution for improving solar energy conversion, especially in high-temperature environments. The analysis revealed that electrical exergy accounted for only 35-40% of the total exergy output, with total exergy efficiency ranging from 5% to 7%. Environmental factors such as solar irradiance, ambient temperature, panel temperature, and wind speed significantly influenced system performance. The integration of 10 TEG modules resulted in a slight increase in the total exergy efficiency by converting part of the waste heat into useful electrical power.

title: How Success Speaks: Configurational Framing in Grant Applications

detail.title: How Success Speaks: Configurational Framing in Grant Applications

detail.abstract: Achieving success is not just about having the idea; how the idea is framed also matters. Prior research has focused primarily on individual textual characteristics rather than framing as an integrated phenomenon. This paper develops a configurational account of framing, arguing that evaluators perceive framing holistically through combinations of characteristics rather than through any single characteristic in isolation. The study draws on 3,955 grant applications submitted to a large European foundation (2015-2019) and 16,830 submitted to the Novo Nordisk Foundation (2018-2025). For each application, I measure twelve textual characteristics using NLP-based semantic models and LIWC. The main analysis identifies eleven framing configurations associated with funding success, consisting of textual characteristics alone or in combination with career stage and scientific field. Each configuration shows a positive superadditivity premium, indicating that the complete configuration is more strongly associated with funding than its individual conditions considered separately. These configurations reflect three broader mechanisms: conventional academic restraint, confident analytical framing, and strategic promotion.

title: Narrative Legitimacy: The Credibility of Institutional Meaning Systems

detail.title: Narrative Legitimacy: The Credibility of Institutional Meaning Systems

declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual theoretical work based on analysis of existing scholarly literature and publicly available organizational examples. It did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal subjects. Accordingly, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Leadership scholars have long recognized that institutional legitimacy is essential for sustaining authority, organizational stability, and collective action. Existing research demonstrates that legitimacy is influenced by legal authority, procedural fairness, institutional performance, and stakeholder perceptions, yet comparatively less attention has been devoted to the interpretive process through which institutions establish and sustain legitimacy by constructing credible and coherent systems of meaning. This paper examines the relationship between institutional legitimacy, organizational sensemaking, and leadership through a conceptual analysis of scholarship on legitimacy theory, organizational institutionalism, and narrative leadership. The analysis identifies a theoretical gap concerning how institutions develop and maintain legitimacy through the credibility and coherence of the narratives that shape collective understanding. To address this gap, the paper develops the concept of Narrative Legitimacy, defined as the perceived credibility and coherence of institutional meaning systems. The analysis argues that institutional legitimacy depends not solely upon legal authority, organizational performance, or procedural compliance, but upon the extent to which institutional narratives provide coherent, credible, and collectively accepted interpretations of organizational reality. By identifying Narrative Legitimacy as a distinct leadership mechanism, this paper extends existing scholarship on institutional legitimacy while contributing a foundational construct to Narrative Power Leadership Theory (NPLT). The findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding how institutional meaning systems sustain organizational credibility, reinforce collective confidence, and support enduring leadership influence under conditions of continuity and change.

title: The Oyster as a Natural Asset: Valuing Carbon Sequestration from Bivalve Aquaculture

detail.title: The Oyster as a Natural Asset: Valuing Carbon Sequestration from Bivalve Aquaculture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none to disclose
declarations.funderStatement: none to disclose

detail.abstract: Recent work valuing the carbon sequestration services of great whales (Chami et al., 2019) established a framework for pricing living organisms as natural capital assets. We extend this framework to farmed bivalves, arguing that aquaculture resolves the additionality problem inherent in wild-animal carbon valuation: a new oyster farm creates sequestration that verifiably would not otherwise occur. Using a discounted cash flow model of a representative 1M-oyster/yr farm, we value three sequestration pathways: gross shell carbon, shell carbon net of calcification CO 2 release, and full ecosystem carbon including sediment organic burial. Monte Carlo simulation (20,000 draws) over contested biophysical and market parameters yields a median 20-year NPV of approximately $39,000 for the full-ecosystem case (P5-P95: $11k-$108k), versus approximately $4,500 for shells alone. Critically, rank-correlation analysis shows the calcification release ratio-the center of the decade-long "source vs. sink" debate-explains almost none of the valuation variance (ρ =-0.04), which is instead dominated by carbon price (ρ = 0.66) and the farm-scale organic burial multiplier (ρ = 0.54). Netting farm operational emissions cuts the median creditable value by two-thirds and implies a ∼24% probability that a typical farm is a net emitter, conceding the direction of the lifecycle critique while preserving positive expected value. We conclude that research and policy attention should shift from shell chemistry to sediment burial verification and farm decarbonization, and outline a credit-methodology pathway modeled on existing bivalve nitrogen-trading programs.

title: Constitutional Copyright and the Meaning of Postponed Matters
affiliations: Loyola Law School Los Angeles

detail.title: Constitutional Copyright and the Meaning of Postponed Matters

declarations.declarationOfInterest: To the best of my knowledge, I do not have any personal or financial relationship with persons or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have improperly influenced the drafting of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
The U.S. Constitution became an inspiration for the writing of organic laws all over the world; its provisions were often copied, its ideas even more often emulated.  That includes Article I, Section, 8, Clause 8 – the mysterious 27 words drafted by the Constitutional Convention’s “Committee on Postponed Matters” that gave Congress the power to grant copyrights and patents. 

Since at least the mid-nineteenth century, American courts have wrestled with the meaning of many of the words in that clause -- “Author,” “Writing,” “Limited Times,” and “Progress” – as well as what boundaries, if any, these words put on Congress’ ability to legislate legal protection for expressive works.  This paper offers a survey of these debates, noting that courts have been decidedly non-originalist when it comes to the Copyright and Patent Clause and that the one occasion when the Supreme Court used the clause to put sharp limits on copyright was a case centered on perceived lower court laxness, not Congressional expansion or strengthening of copyright.

Given the sparse historical record on the drafting of the Copyright and Patent Clause, this paper critiques various assumptions on how the clause was composed and emphasizes the speculative nature of any claims on the clause’s meaning.

detail.abstract: The aim of this study is to explore how Swedish sustainability reports can serve as a reference point for Bosnia and Herzegovina in building a more coherent and comparable reporting system. This study focuses on sustainability reports from Swedish listed companies aligned with the CSRD as a benchmark for Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2024. By conducting a comparative and content analysis highlight how the structured and detailed form of Swedish reports can inform the development of BiH's practices, which at present lack consistency and formalization. The findings suggest that implementing the CSRD could accelerate BiH's transition toward systematic and internationally comparable reporting. The paper concludes on how Swedish experiences and reporting practices can be adapted to the Bosnian context. The findings indicate that Swedish reports are characterized by a high degree of standardization, sectoral comparability, and integration with European sustainability frameworks, while Bosnian reports show inconsistency and limited stakeholder orientation. The study concludes that gradual adoption of the CSRD, accompanied by institutional support and sector-specific guidelines, could accelerate Bosnia and Herzegovina's transition toward systematic, transparent, and internationally comparable reporting. Swedish experiences thus offer concrete lessons for designing a more coherent sustainability reporting system in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

detail.abstract: Historical off-policy evaluation (OPE) is useful for deployment only when the available evidence can resolve a policy decision, not merely estimate policy values with moderate accuracy. We study this distinction with QQQ, SPY, and IWM in a one-step contextual-bandit design. OPE receives partial-feedback logs generated by a common Thompson-sampling logger, while the price-taking structure allows all three one-step action rewards to be reconstructed after the next return is observed and withheld for scoring. Under a frozen cross-ETF protocol, all available pre-anchor history gives lower doubly robust (DR) mean absolute error than trailing 252-, 126-, and 60-observation windows for every ETF. Yet even under this best-performing evidence rule, median candidate-baseline gaps are only 0.26-0.35 basis points versus paired bootstrap standard errors of 1.86-3.42 basis points; point-estimate policy selection is near 50%, and an approximate 95% one-sided lower-confidence rule admits the candidate in only about 2-3% of evaluation windows. Improving target-policy action coverage raises effective sample size by 3.33-3.84% at 𝑚 = 80, but lowers MAE by only 0.71-1.86%. The central finding is therefore decision-based: more history and better overlap can improve standard OPE diagnostics without making a close policy comparison resolvable. Historical OPE should distinguish value accuracy, action support, and policy-gap resolution, and should permit evidence-based abstention when the logged data do not justify a switch.

title: Incentives for Foreign Investors under Nigeria Tax Act

detail.title: Incentives for Foreign Investors under Nigeria Tax Act

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nil
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 introduced a new framework for taxation in Nigeria and significantly altered the legal framework for the tax incentives available to companies and investors in Nigeria. This article examines these tax incentives under the Act that may be relevant to foreign investors who seek to establish or expand business operations in Nigeria. Using a doctrinal research methodology, the article analyses the relevant provisions of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 alongside other applicable legislation and examines the conditions governing the availability of these incentives. It clarifies the distinction between incentives that are specifically targeted at foreign investors and those that are generally available to taxpayers but may still be beneficial to foreign investors seeking to invest in Nigeria. The article further considers the conditions attached to these incentives and the extent to which incentives under the former regime remain relevant following the commencement of the new tax laws. It also highlights the uncertainty surrounding the treatment of foreign-owned Nigerian companies in relation to the exemption from the development levy. The article argues that the existence of a tax incentive does not automatically guarantee eligibility and that the practical benefit available to a foreign investor ultimately depends on the nature of the investment, the structure of the business and compliance with the statutory conditions governing the relevant incentive.

detail.title: Experience and Pivoting in Entrepreneurial Product Development

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Pivoting is a significant shift from the current product under development to an alternative opportunity. Pivoting is strongly advocated in the popular press and is commonly used in entrepreneurial product development. However, a high proportion of startups that pivot fail subsequently, since many entrepreneurs chase pivots that are ultimately not fruitful. We explore how an entrepreneur's level of experience influences the decision to pivot. Experienced entrepreneurs, possessing a clearer perception of potential obstacles and opportunities, tend to exhibit reduced overconfidence. 
Methodology/results: We develop a decision-theoretic model to analyze the entrepreneurial choice regarding pivoting, while accounting for overconfidence and market and pivot opportunity uncertainties. We show that lack of experience, i.e., a higher level of overconfidence, can systematically influence pivoting decisions. The effect of overconfidence on a pivot decision depends on the market uncertainty of the pivot opportunity relative to that of the already initiated product. More specifically, we show that novice (more overconfident) entrepreneurs are likely to make radical risky pivots, whereas experienced (less overconfident) entrepreneurs are more likely to make safe pivots. We find that the dominant development errors for inexperienced founders relate to pivoting and persisting when faced with risky and safe pivots, respectively. Furthermore, we show that if pivoting can be postponed until after the product launch, novice founders are more likely to postpone safe pivots than experienced founders. We also explore the effects of different types of experience on the entrepreneur's pivoting decisions. 
Managerial implications: Our results can benefit entrepreneurs in deciding how to set the duration of their supply chain contracts, choose the types of employees to hire, and select appropriate mentors, based on the experience level of the founders and their likely pivot behavior. For startup incubators and accelerators, our results indicate what type of training programs to provide for entrepreneurs when accounting for their experience level.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the transformation of the accounting profession, focusing on the evolving role of accountants in the digital era. As digital technologies automate traditional accounting tasks, the profession must redefine its relevance within modern organizations. Accountants are increasingly expected to combine financial expertise with technological competence, participating in the development of accounting information systems and using digital tools for the preparation, analysis, and visual presentation of financial data. These changes reinforce the importance of collaboration between accountants and management in data-driven decision-making processes. The paper presents empirical findings on the digital readiness of accountants in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH). It analyses their competencies, the extent of organizational support for digital training, and the adequacy of the educational framework in preparing them for technological transformation. The results provide insights and recommendations aimed at strengthening the strategic position of accountants in the digital environment. Moreover, the study highlights the blurred boundaries between accounting and information technology, where new responsibilities lack clear professional ownership. It argues that accountants should view digitalization not as a threat, but as an opportunity to expand their professional influence and reaffirm their role in shaping the future of the accounting profession.

detail.title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Clean Energy Markets in China
detail.abstract: The relationship between China’s clean energy markets and China’s climate policy uncertainty (CCPU) has generally been considered weak in the literature. We challenge this view by examining the degree and structure of dependence between CCPU and the returns of six clean energy sub-industry indices, including solar, nuclear, wind, new energy vehicles, fuel cell, and smart grid, over the period 2010-2025. Using a quantile regression approach, we find that although mean-based models indicate a weak relationship, the CCPU-return dependence does exist but varies across the distribution. In particular, the dependence is more pronounced in the middle to upper quantiles (50%-90%). At the sector level, the solar industry is the only sector to display a negative dependence with CCPU in the lower tail of the return distribution (25%), while such a relationship is pervasive in higher tails across the sectors. Our subperiod analysis shows that the dependence between CCPU and clean energy returns is time-varying. The Paris Agreement period (2016-2019) exhibits a higher degree of dependence and a stronger dependence structure in most sectors, whereas the COVID-19 period (2020-2021) is characterized by stronger short-term co-movement but less stable patterns. Our findings provide new evidence that the relationship between CCPU and clean energy sub-industry returns is heterogeneous across quantiles, sectors, and event periods, with important implications for portfolio diversification, risk management, and climate-related financial policy.​

title: Adieu Terroir - The Global Drift of Geographical indications Law
affiliations: Loyola Law School Los Angeles

detail.title: Adieu Terroir - The Global Drift of Geographical indications Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: To the best of my knowledge, I do not have any personal or financial relationship with persons or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have improperly influenced this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
The law of appellations of origin (appellations d’origine controle) was built on the mysterious, but intuitively appealing idea of terroir - that a particular place – its soil, climate, and agricultural traditions -- produces specific product characteristics that cannot be easily imitated elsewhere.  The terroir made each product protected by an appellation – and later a geographical indication – unique, even if consumers could not always tell the difference.  Of course, this implicitly supported thinking that some places and some products were inherently better than other places and other products.

When a framework for protection of geographical indications (GIs) was built into the 1994 TRIPS Agreement, the notion of terroir was still present, but was already fading.   But as GI proponents have advocated for sui generis GI laws globally, they have sought to generalize the appeal of such laws, moving GI law further and further away from a terroir foundation and ever closer to a kind of certification mark law in which the state plays a significant regulatory and often managerial role.  Nowhere is this conceptual shift more evident than in the move to protect artisanal works and handicrafts with GI law.

The paper explores both the indicia and reasons for this conceptual evolution, discussing the GI provisions of the European Union’s bilateral free trade agreements, GIs for crafts and industrial products, and the existential threat to terroir posed by climate change.  Overall the global shift is one in which GI law is becoming less mysterious, more egalitarian, and more akin to trademark law.

detail.abstract: This paper asks two questions. Which institutional characteristics are associated with stronger or weaker campus speech climates? And do institutions take corrective action when they are publicly ranked near the bottom? A university faces two costs of restricting speech: a legal cost that binds only public institutions, and a reputational cost is paid when its climate is publicly observed and private institutions also bear this cost. The evidence comes from five waves of the FIRE College Free Speech Rankings, 1,112 institution-waves covering 257 colleges from 2022 to 2026, merged with IPEDS. On the first question, being a public institution is the strongest institutional correlate of a strong speech climate among a plethora of institutional characteristics such as size, selectivity, wealth, religious affiliation and student ideology. On the second, institutions do respond, and the response grows with how conspicuous the bad rank was. Those placed in the bottom quintile of a wave are four times as likely than the best-ranked quintile to upgrade FIRE's written speech-code rating in the next wave as the low ranking causes reputational damage. Private institutions respond at least as strongly as public ones. Reputational accountability therefore reaches institutions the First Amendment does not. This suggests that broader and more salient disclosure is a market-based alternative to government regulation of campus speech.

detail.abstract: The sustainability of Nigeria's indigenous oil and gas service companies depends largely on their ability to attract, develop, and retain a competent workforce capable of supporting local content objectives and maintaining operational competitiveness. Despite the enactment of the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development (NOGICD) Act to strengthen indigenous participation through workforce development, many indigenous companies continue to experience persistent talent loss arising from inadequate investment in employee training and professional development. This study investigates how insufficient training and upskilling programmes influence talent retention in indigenous oil and gas service companies, using Geomarine Systems Limited in Rivers State, Nigeria, as a qualitative single-case study. Guided by Human Capital Theory and the Resource-Based View, the study explores employees' perceptions of training adequacy, the organizational consequences of limited training opportunities, and strategies for improving workforce retention. Data were collected through structured interviews with employees occupying technical, operational, administrative, and managerial positions and analysed using thematic analysis supported by NVivo software. The findings revealed that inadequate training opportunities weaken employee commitment, reduce job satisfaction, limit career progression, and significantly contribute to talent turnover. Furthermore, limited investment in workforce development constrains organizational productivity and undermines compliance with national and local content objectives. The study contributes to the literature by integrating Human Capital Theory and the Resource-Based View within the Nigerian indigenous oil and gas context, while offering practical recommendations for strengthening employee development initiatives. These include structured career pathways, leadership accountability, and institutionalised learning systems to support sustainable performance and long-term talent retention in indigenous firms.

title: The Climate Component of World Productivity Growth: A Quintipartite Production-Frontier Decomposition

detail.title: The Climate Component of World Productivity Growth: A Quintipartite Production-Frontier Decomposition

detail.abstract: We provide the first whole-economy production-frontier decomposition of labor productivity growth with a climate component, extending the Kumar-Russell-Henderson-Russell growth-accounting program to five margins: efficiency change, technical change, physical and human capital deepening, and climate. Because climate-conditional frontiers estimated from the cross-section absorb everything correlated with latitude-implying hot-zone damages an order of magnitude above quasi-experimental estimates-we discipline the climate margin with a gradient identified from within-country, first-differenced variation, preserving the decomposition's exact multiplicativity. Across 96 countries, observed warming (1.2 • C on average) reduced world labor productivity by 0.4 percent over 1971-2019 (95% CI [0.1, 0.7]); cold countries gained, hot countries lost, and 71 percent of countries were net-damaged. Magnitudes scale with the identifying horizon-decadal long differences imply damages seven times larger-bracketing the weather-versus-climate debate rather than adjudicating it. Climate change has pushed against convergence: its component correlates at-0.73 with baseline temperature and +0.38 with income, transferring productivity from poor-hot to rich-cold countries, though it has not reshaped the world distribution, which capital deepening and nonneutral technical change still govern. Technical change is itself climatically localized: a-0.5 percent per • C association of frontier shifts with baseline temperature survives conditioning on capital intensity.

title: Selection Look-Ahead Is Not a Data Problem: Measuring the Leak in a Screening Rule's Labels

detail.title: Selection Look-Ahead Is Not a Data Problem: Measuring the Leak in a Screening Rule's Labels

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author sells the pairs screen studied in this paper as a subscription product (PairDesk) and operates a commercial backtest-audit practice. The result reported here is printed on the product's own page. No other person or organization influenced the study.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. The research was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: A screen chooses candidates on a window of history. When it then reports an "out-of-sample" result on the last part of that same window, the future has leaked into the choosing, even if every statistic inside the screen was computed walk-forward. We measure this leak on a weekly pairs screen that tests about 1.7 million combinations of liquid US stocks and ETFs. When every accept-or-reject decision is recomputed inside each test year, so that no decision can see the year it is judged on, the screen's apparent edge disappears: the gap between accepted pairs and correlation-matched rejected pairs falls from about eleven log points a year to slightly below zero. Splitting the pairs accepted in-era by one bit of future information, whether the full-window rule would also have accepted them, isolates the leak: that bit is worth about fourteen log points a year, more than the edge that had been measured. A positive control shows the same code recovering a planted edge, and a prevalence sweep bounds what the clean test could have missed. The protocol is released as a check in an open-source package, with a within-era permutation test in place of sign counts, and placebo labels are shown to read clean. The finding concerns a rule's labels, not pairs trading; the commercial screens examined share the construction that produces it.

title: Wildfire Risk Capitalization as a Coupled Hazard-Housing System: A State-Channel-Phase Framework and Systematic Critical Review of U.S. Evidence

detail.title: Wildfire Risk Capitalization as a Coupled Hazard-Housing System: A State-Channel-Phase Framework and Systematic Critical Review of U.S. Evidence

detail.abstract: Wildfire housing studies often treat burned, nearby, mapped, smoke-exposed, difficult-to-insure, and mitigated properties as observations of the same shock. This systematic critical review asks how wildfire hazard is transmitted through housing markets and when an observed price sign diverges from household loss. OpenAlex and Crossref searches, supplemented by documented citation chasing, produced 2,300 screened records. Forty-three U.S.-focused publication families were critically appraised: 32 supplied wildfire-resolvable core residential-market evidence and 11 supplied mechanism, policy, or boundary-setting evidence. Because exposures, outcomes, spatial contrasts, horizons, and samples were not exchangeable, the review did not pool estimates. Instead, it advances a state-channel-phase framework that cross-classifies six exposure states, five transmission channels (physical loss, amenity and information, insurance and credit, supply and displacement, and stock composition), and three phases (anticipation, immediate shock, and adjustment or recovery). Five falsifiable propositions follow. They predict attenuation under coarse exposure measures, migration of risk from prices into insurance or credit, post-fire sign inversions caused by scarcity and rebuilding selection, a wedge between physical and market returns to mitigation, and complementarities among disclosure, insurance, mitigation, and safer supply. The evidence explains why rising prices of surviving or rebuilt homes can coexist with destruction, displacement, and incomplete recovery. The framework advances natural-hazard research by replacing sign-only synthesis with diagnostic estimands and testable mechanisms for coupled hazard-housing systems.

title: Successful Rescue and the Loss of Organizational Evidence: Consequence Integrity in Organizations

detail.title: Successful Rescue and the Loss of Organizational Evidence: Consequence Integrity in Organizations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests relevant to this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper and did not involve human participants, patient data, or an empirical dataset.

detail.abstract: Organizations often treat successful rescue as evidence of resilience: the deadline holds, the case closes, the customer never sees the failure. This paper asks what happens when rescue succeeds so completely that the organization loses evidence of what had to be rescued. I develop Consequence Integrity, a system property describing whether material consequences remain visible after local resolution, traceable to what produced them, and connected to sufficient resolution capacity to revise the source or explicitly own the remaining cost. The argument sits inside a broader Integrity Load Theory (ILT) and links a sequence of decision, remainder, migration, carrier, rescue, apparent success, and return or lock-in. The paper does not claim that workarounds, invisible work, resilience, organizational learning, or silence are new phenomena. Instead, it confronts adjacent literatures directly and asks whether consequence migration and return add explanatory value beyond them. Five propositions predict when rescue should reduce source visibility, when burden should concentrate in stable carriers, why senior escalation without sufficient resolution capacity should fail to produce source revision, when return should interrupt lock-in, and why an acknowledged remainder should preserve more Consequence Integrity than an erased one. Boundary conditions and falsification tests are stated explicitly. The central claim is deliberately narrow: rescue becomes structurally dangerous when repeated private compensation preserves the expected outcome while erasing the route by which that outcome was actually achieved.

detail.abstract: Border-county difference-indifferences (DiD) analysis is widely used to evaluate state policies, but demographic differences across borders may threaten identification and external validity when treatment effects vary by demographic group. We examine U.S. border-county composition using 2022 American Community Survey data. In percentage point terms, border counties are 1.9 more White, 1.3 less Black, and 1.8 less Hispanic than nonborder counties, with differences up to 38.6 across some state borders. We demonstrate the empirical importance of these differences by analyzing the 2014 ACA Medicaid expansion's effects on health insurance coverage. We find substantial heterogeneity in treatment effects by race and ethnicity, with pooled estimates masking this variation and failing to represent the true effect for any specific demographic group. When demographic composition differs across borders and treatment effects vary by demographics, pooled estimates conflate compositional differences with true treatment effects. Researchers should test for parallel trends by subgroup, estimate heterogeneous treatment effects where feasible, and report border-county demographics to assess external validity.

title:
Monopoly, Moligopoly and the Missing Jurisdiction

A review of Nicolas Petit, Big Tech and the Digital Economy: The Moligopoly Scenario

Monopoly, Moligopoly and the Missing Jurisdiction

A review of Nicolas Petit, Big Tech and the Digital Economy: The Moligopoly Scenario

declarations.funderStatement: SELF FUNDING

detail.abstract:
Nicolas Petit published this book at the high-water mark of the techlash. Legislatures on both sides of the Atlantic were preparing structural reform, agencies were assembling monopolisation cases, and a broad consensus held that the largest technology firms were the trusts of the present century. The book’s intervention was not to defend those firms but to interrogate the premise on which the consensus rested: that a durable position in a market without close rivals is, without more, monopoly.

The answer Petit proposes is ‘moligopoly’, a coinage fusing monopoly and oligopoly. The claim is that the six firms he studies — Microsoft, Apple, Google, Netflix, Amazon and Facebook — may be structural monopolists in the markets where they originated and, at the same time, oligopolists engaged in intense rivalry with each other and with unknown entrants in markets that have not yet tipped. The prescriptive consequence is a recalibration: competition law should concentrate on markets that have already tipped, adopt a lighter touch where they have not, and leave privacy, disinformation and hate speech to regulation rather than to antitrust.

This review advances three arguments. First, the book’s most durable contribution is evidentiary rather than theoretical: its use of securities disclosures and analyst material as evidence about competitive constraint deserves to outlive the argument about its conclusions. Second, the years since publication have supplied something that a book about uncertainty rarely receives — a natural experiment — and the results are genuinely divided. The moligopoly thesis has fared markedly better at the remedies stage than at the liability stage. Third, the framework carries a jurisdictional blind spot. Its central prescriptive distinction, between tipped and untipped markets, presupposes market and institutional conditions that much of the world does not have. In Sri Lanka, neither limb of Petit’s prescription is presently available.

detail.abstract: Management-friendly governance arrangements are often viewed as manifestations of weak governance that enable rent extraction. We show that such arrangements may arise endogenously as an efficient response to a commitment problem induced by transferable ownership. When shareholders can sell their claims before the long-run outcomes of managerial actions are realized, anticipated resale weakens commitment to long-term investment. In response, shareholders optimally cede bargaining power over compensation design to managers, despite the higher managerial rents this may entail. Nevertheless, severe shareholder short-termism limits the extent to which relinquishing bargaining power restores commitment to long-term investment. The optimal transfer of power is therefore non-monotonic, peaking at an intermediate degree of ownership instability. Consequently, governance constraints on managerial bargaining power may have a perverse effect on investment efficiency, and limited compensation disclosure can further exacerbate underinvestment relative to contract opacity.

title: Geometric and Arithmetic Likelihood Aggregation for Diffusions with Heterogeneous Volatility

detail.abstract: Two orderings of Kullback-Leibler divergence lead to different aggregation rules for expert diffusion models. Candidate-first minimization gives a normalized geometric pool, while expert-first minimization is selected by weighted expected logarithmic wealth and gives the arithmetic mixture. The latter remains defined for diffusion laws with different quadratic variation but is generally not itself a Markov diffusion. To obtain diffusion-valued aggregates when expert covariance specifications differ, we introduce an information-transport divergence whose drift term is the local Kullback-Leibler rate associated with a Girsanov change of drift and whose covariance term is the Bures-Wasserstein distance. The expert-first problem yields a Markov projection of the arithmetic mixture. Its drift is the state-posterior mean of expert drifts, and its covariance balances Bures-Wasserstein proximity against an inverse-covariance penalty generated by drift dispersion. The candidate-first problem is a controlled diffusion characterized by a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. It recovers the common-covariance Kullback-Leibler barycenter and the deterministic Gaussian adapted-transport problem as limiting cases. We prove a matrix congruence representation for the covariance selector and show that I + λ-1 D 2 V ≻ 0 is the exact finiteness condition for the unrestricted local problem. A linear-quadratic model shows that drift disagreement lowers the candidate-first covariance selector but raises the expert-first selector. Exact Ornstein-Uhlenbeck transitions and localized stationary square-root calculations identify additional coupling and boundary effects.

detail.abstract: Peripheral in economic and demographic terms throughout colonial history, the Amazon underwent a major transformation during the first wave of globalization (1850-1914). Thanks to the growing external demand for rubber-which became Brazil's second most important export product by the end of the 19th century-the region began to attract capital and workers, government revenues increased, and its main cities benefited from some of the advancements that characterized the Belle Époque. It is therefore surprising to readers of documents from the time to find repeated criticisms-made even by the leaders of the provinces of Pará and Amazonas-regarding the harmful consequences of extractive activity, particularly the issue of productive overspecialization. Bárbara Weinstein links such criticisms to a conflict between old and new elites, a hypothesis we consider insufficient to fully explain the phenomenon. Based on an analysis of contemporary documents, we show that both the criticism and the defense of the sector aligned with relevant points in economic theory, and that the dominance of one perspective or the other seems to depend on the economic context experienced by the provinces.

title: Can Sovereign Debt Early-warning Dashboards be Validated? Evidence from a Declared Walk-forward

detail.abstract: Sovereign debt "dashboards"-indicator panels that color a country's fiscal position green, yellow, or red-implicitly claim that combinations of fiscal, monetary, and external gauges provide early warning of disorderly debt adjustment. We test whether that claim can be validated on the evidence base it invokes: the long-run advanced-economy panel. Using the Jordà-Schularick-Taylor Macrohistory Database, Release 6 (18 countries, 1870-2020; Jordà, Schularick, and Taylor 2017), we define disorderlyadjustment onsets mechanically from declared rules, construct thirteen declared indicators under an enforced look-ahead gate, and run an expanding-window walk-forward comparing a multi-indicator model against debt/GDP alone. The design identifies 34 onsets over 2,548 risk-set country-years (1.33% annual incidence), of which ten fall after 1950. The walk-forward can score seven of those ten: the declared eight-fold grid sees four onsets (eight lead rows in one window); a post-hoc tiling of test windows, reported alongside the declared grid, sees seven onsets (21 lead rows in four windows). Two onsets are invisible by construction-a repeat six years after a prior onset has every three-year lead row inside the previous exclusion window-and one sits in a fold-boundary gap. A 0.10 AUC gap would want about 45-110 independent positives (Hanley and McNeil 1982; 80% power, two-sided 5%, score correlation 0.3-0.7); the post-1950 record contains ten. Advanced-economy disorderly adjustments are too rare for multi-indicator early-warning claims to be validated out of sample on the panel such dashboards implicitly cite. The decision timeline-what was locked, when, and what was refused after results were visible-is a central exhibit, because the finding is only as strong as the discipline that produced it.

title: Major Acquisitions under Nigerian Law: An Interpretative Conundrum

detail.title: Major Acquisitions under Nigerian Law: An Interpretative Conundrum

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Section 342(1) of the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 (CAMA) presents a significant interpretative conundrum concerning the regulatory proviso(s) for major acquisitions in Nigeria. While the provision expressly subjects acquisitions which fall outside the usual course of a company's business to the major asset transaction regime, it is ambiguous as to whether the accompanying 50% book value threshold applies to such acquisitions or exclusively to dispositions. This ambiguity has given rise to divergent interpretations among practitioners, potentially subjecting transactions of negligible value to the procedural requirements applicable to major asset transactions. This essay critically examines the conflicting interpretations of section 342(1)(a) and (b), applying a purposive and jurisprudential approach to determine the proper construction of the provision. It argues that the 50% book value threshold should be construed as applicable to both major acquisitions and major sales. This interpretation avoids the absurdity and unnecessary bureaucracy that would result from treating immaterial acquisitions as major transactions, and establishes greater coherence in the regulation of acquisitions and dispositions. 

A juxtaposition of 342(1) with the corresponding provisions of the Mauritian Companies Act 2001 and the New Zealand Companies Act 1993, further supports this construction. This paper recommends legislative clarification of section 342(1) and, pending such amendment, proposes a contractual and corporate governance workarounds.

title: The Statistical Measurement and Impact Effects of Lithium Resource Supply Chain Security
affiliations: Beijing Technology and Business University and Beijing Technology and Business University

detail.title: The Statistical Measurement and Impact Effects of Lithium Resource Supply Chain Security
detail.abstract: The accelerating transition to low-carbon energy systems has elevated lithium to a strategically vital mineral, particularly for electric vehicle propulsion and stationary battery storage. As the dominant global processor and end-user of lithium compounds, China is confronting mounting supply-chain fragilities stemming from heavy reliance on foreign ores, elevated supplier concentration, intensifying great-power rivalry, and recurrent price gyrations. A thorough quantitative understanding of how these stressors emerge and transmit across the industrial chain is urgently needed. In response, this investigation designs a multi-faceted evaluation framework for lithium supply security (LSSI) spanning 2010--2024, anchored in the Availability--Accessibility--Affordability--Acceptability (4A) paradigm and operationalised through fourteen sub-indicators weighted via a combined entropy-AHP scheme. Exploiting this infrastructure, we execute four complementary inquiries: a longitudinal mapping of the international lithium trade web, a dynamic tracking of China's LSSI trajectory, a structural decomposition of lithium price disturbances along the NEV value chain using recursive VAR/SVAR identification, and a cross-sectional panel analysis covering fifteen representative economies. China's LSSI exhibits a pronounced W-shaped fluctuation, bottoming out during the 2022 price shock before staging a recovery. Econometrically, geopolitical tensions, import reliance, market concentration, and price instability all exert statistically and economically meaningful downward pressures on LSSI, whereas enhanced recycling capacity and proactive industrial policies generate offsetting uplifts. A mediation exercise further establishes that import costs serve as a key conduit through which geopolitical frictions impair security outcomes. These results offer actionable intelligence for policy-makers aiming to fortify critical-mineral supply chains via supply-base diversification, circular-economy initiatives, strategic stockpiling, and sustained technological innovation.

title: Measuring What Matters: Honest Evidence and Good Governance in the Arts

detail.abstract: Performing arts and cultural organizations across Europe and the United States face severe financial pressure, demographic change, and rapid technological disruption. The standard responses involve appeals for more public money, calls for new audiences, and exhortations to «innovate». This article argues that an important governance reform for the sector is a discipline of honest measurement: institutions should know whether their programs advance the artistic, cultural, social, public, and economic purposes they claim to serve. Measurement is not a fundraising device or an import of business metrics; it is part of mission stewardship, public accountability, and organizational learning. Drawing on recent research in the economics of art and culture-including new European evidence that artists face persistent wage and job-quality penalties even in systems with substantial public cultural funding-the article develops a proportional «evidence ladder» that matches evaluative expectations to organizational capacity, and closes with a practical checklist for boards, funders, and public agencies, attentive to Greek and continental European contexts where public value and cultural legitimacy, rather than philanthropy, anchor the case for evidence.

detail.title: Technical–profit efficiency divergence in China's industrial sector: The role of allocative efficiency under shadow pricing
detail.abstract: Given that environmental constraints on China’s industrial sector are increasingly reflected in explicit factor prices and pollution abatement operational costs, eco-efficiency assessments based solely on technological feasibility may overestimate actual performance under cost constraints. This study combines a radial data envelopment analysis model with a Farrell-type profit-efficiency framework to jointly evaluate technical efficiency (TE), profit efficiency (PE), and allocative efficiency (AE). The model incorporates both desirable outputs and undesirable byproducts of industrial production and introduces exogenously constructed shadow prices as proxies for abatement costs. Empirical analysis using provincial panel data from 2017–2022 reveals significant spatial heterogeneity: coastal provinces and municipalities consistently achieve frontier performance in both TE and PE, while inland provinces exhibit substantial performance gaps. The decomposition shows that the TE–PE divergence is reflected in substantial allocative inefficiency, indicating that mismatches between input–emission allocation and the imposed price system are an important source of profit-oriented eco-efficiency loss. Tobit model analysis further shows that industrial structure, trade openness, and economic development significantly enhance AE, while the positive impact of power supply structure is only marginal. Technology-related fiscal inputs are associated with short-term resource allocation pressures, displaying heterogeneous effects across provinces with different levels of coal dependence. These findings provide systematic evidence on the causes of eco-efficiency losses and offer policy-relevant insights for optimizing regional industrial eco-efficiency.

detail.abstract:
This research monograph examines Washington, DC’s built structural geography through a fixed and reproducible geospatial method. It asks whether the city’s principal concentrations of structurally intense development form one continuous system, how disconnected concentrations relate to one another, and how documented development projects could change that topology.

Structural Intensity is calculated from Microsoft’s 2023 Q4 estimated building-footprint coverage and normalized building-height raster. Native raster cells qualify at the fixed threshold of SI ≥ 0.007987 and are grouped using strict 8-neighbor connectivity, without smoothing, gap filling, artificial bridging, or manual component merging. Threshold-sensitivity testing, independent building-footprint and height comparisons, orthophotography, parcel geometry, documented project envelopes, and a formal post-calibration threshold audit are used to assess stability and external credibility.

The results support a polycentric interpretation of Washington, DC’s most structurally intense built form. The Structural Core is the largest connected qualifying component, while eight substantive components south of the National Mall remain disconnected in the observed 2023 Q4 topology. Project-envelope testing identifies One K Street SW as the strongest documented near-term structural change, while other project scenarios retain explicitly differentiated evidence statuses. The monograph also introduces a four-stage Structural Evolution Framework for distinguishing observed topology from modeled structural connection, reinforcement, and maturation.

title: Tax Enforcement, Gutted: Tax Lawyers' Duties when the Revenue System is under Attack
affiliations: UC Law, San Francisco

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: UC Law San Francisco

detail.abstract: The Trump administration has been gutting the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). The workforce and budget cuts are far more severe than ever before and are likely to create long-lasting harm to the IRS's enforcement ability. That reduces revenue collections and increases economic incentives for cheating. The dismantling of the IRS, together with escalating politicization of the IRS and political leaders whose actions demonstrate disregard for the tax laws, erode public confidence in the tax system and degrade tax morale. That could create noncompliance norms that, once established, will be difficult to reverse. This is all part of the Trump administration's larger assault on legal institutions and the rule of law more generally. These developments demand a recalibration of tax lawyers' ethical responsibilities. Ample literature discusses tax lawyers' ethical duties, but this Article is the first to grapple with the fundamental question about what it should mean to be a tax lawyer when the IRS, the revenue system, and rule of law are under attack as they have been since early 2025 and as they may be for years to come. Ultimately, this Article argues that tax lawyers must play a stronger gatekeeping role going forward and that standards of practice applicable to tax advisors should be raised accordingly. Tax lawyers must stand up for the revenue system and the rule of law. Otherwise, tax lawyers will be complicit in their collapse.

title: How might Neural Networks Work?

detail.title: How might Neural Networks Work?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Deep neural networks repeatedly transform high-dimensional states into internal representations, yet there is no single accepted account of what information an intermediate representation should preserve or how training might favor such information. We develop a target-sufficient perspective based on sharp partial identification. Let an unknown state or path law belong to a stated compatibility class and let Ψ denote the task target. A representation is evaluated not by how faithfully it reconstructs the full state, but by the set of target values that remain compatible with the information it retains. This yields a target identified set and a scalar identification width.
A data-processing result shows that deterministic post-processing cannot shrink this identified set. Hence a useful compression is one that lowers representation cost while introducing little or no additional target ambiguity. The scope of this statement is explicit: a training support can be strictly smaller than the admissible environment domain, so support-local sufficiency need not imply domain-robust sufficiency. We then connect the representation principle to an exact mathematical architecture for partially observed continuous systems: target-relevant features can remove ambient dimensions without loss; finite-memory path targets admit exact automaton augmentation; compatible laws can be propagated by local measure flows rather than complete path enumeration; and genuinely nonlinear restrictions that factor through finitely many law-level moments can be isolated in a low-dimensional moment space with certified global bounds. In validated numerical problems, an empirical formulation retains 3,400 optimization variables as ambient dimension increases from 512 to 16,384, while continuous approximation and hard-support errors admit explicit certificates.
We further ask how ordinary backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent could be compatible with this architecture. Standard chain-rule identities imply a target-sensitive pullback: directions in the local null space of the downstream Jacobian are first-order silent to the task loss on the sampled support. For dense affine layers, a single-sample weight update is an outer product of a forward activation and a backward error signal, and a batch update has rank at most the batch size. These identities do not prove that nuisance information is removed, that task-equivalent histories collapse, or that training loss equals identification width. Instead they motivate additional, falsifiable hypotheses involving contraction of task-equivalent distinctions and alignment between the training direction and reduction of target identification width. The resulting viewpoint complements information-bottleneck, state-abstraction, predictive-state, implicit-bias, and representation-similarity approaches while preserving a sharp distinction between local training evidence and domain-level target sufficiency.

title: Are Two Better than One? The Role of Country Pairs in Multinational Tax Planning

detail.title: Are Two Better than One? The Role of Country Pairs in Multinational Tax Planning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: We examine the individual countries and pairs of countries where foreign subsidiaries have the greatest effect on U.S. multinational corporations' (MNCs) tax burdens. We hypothesize that locating subsidiaries in combinations of foreign countries results in incremental tax planning opportunities. We find that well-known tax haven countries are associated with lower cash ETRs. However, we also find that countries traditionally considered less tax-friendly are associated with lower cash ETRs. We then find that country pairs are associated with lower cash ETRs and that the top country pairs yield approximately three times larger cash ETR impacts than the top individual countries. Finally, we document that the individual countries and country pairs associated with lower cash ETRs vary across time and based on where firms have most of their foreign sales. By considering the role of country pairs, we document the effect of complex operational decisions where firms strategically source income across their affiliates.

title: The Racial Wage Gap and Task Segregation

detail.title: The Racial Wage Gap and Task Segregation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that no competing interests exist.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no specific funding for this work.

detail.abstract: Despite substantial wage convergence between Black and White workers prior to 1980, the racial wage gap has since stagnated and even widened. This paper examines how much of this widening the occupational task structure accounts for, and whether it operates through shifts in task allocation between the two groups (task sorting) or through changes in the return to tasks (task prices). I find that racial disparities in task allocation have narrowed, reducing the gap. However, I find that this progress has been outpaced by a sharp rise in the Social task price. White men disproportionately benefited from the increased Social task price because Black men still remain underrepresented in Social-intensive occupations. To identify the specific Social tasks behind this price effect, I use machine learning to construct a data-driven task classification. I find that the widening gap is not driven by Coordination-Social tasks, such as management and scheduling, but by Analytical-Social tasks, such as analyzing and interpreting information for others. Together, these results suggest that racially neutral changes in task price are now the central mechanism widening the racial wage gap.

title: Structural Tensions in the Bitcoin Protocol: A Conditional Trilemma Treatment of Throughput, Security-budget, Centralization, and Cryptographic-longevity Constraints

detail.title: Structural Tensions in the Bitcoin Protocol: A Conditional Trilemma Treatment of Throughput, Security-budget, Centralization, and Cryptographic-longevity Constraints

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
